seaward: Directed or situated toward the sea. Donne. Two still clouds . . . sparkled on their seaward edges like a frosted fleece. G. W. Cable.
separatrix: The decimal point; the dot placed at the left of a decimal fraction, to separate it from the whole number which it follows. The term is sometimes also applied to other marks of separation.
sexual: Of or pertaining to sex, or the sexes; distinguishing sex; peculiar to the distinction and office of male or female; relating to the distinctive genital organs of the sexes; proceeding from, or based upon, sex; as, sexual characteristics; sexual intercourse, connection, or commerce; sexual desire; sexual diseases; sexual generation.
septentrion: The north or northern regions. Shak. Both East West, South and Septentrioun. Chaucer. | Of or pertaining to the north; northern. "From cold septentrion blasts." Milton.
seaholly: An evergeen seashore plant (Eryngium maritimum). See Eryngium.
sealanguage: The peculiar language or phraseology of seamen; sailor's cant.
setbolt: 1. An iron pin, or bolt, for fitting planks closely together. Craig. 2. A bolt used for forcing another bolt out of its hole.
sentimentality: The quality or state of being sentimental.
semisaxon: Half Saxon; -- specifically applied to the language intermediate between Saxon and English, belonging to the period 1150- 1250.
seniorize: To exercise authority; to rule; to lord it. Fairfax.
seron: Same as Ceroon. Note: This word as expressing a quantity or weight has no definite signification. McElrath.
serbonian: Relating to the lake of Serbonis in Egypt, which by reason of the sand blowing into it had a deceptive appearance of being solid land, but was a bog. A gulf profound as that Serbonian bog . . . Where armies whole have sunk. Milton.
semipelagian: A follower of John Cassianus, a French monk (died about 448), who modified the doctrines of Pelagius, by denying human merit, and maintaining the necessity of the Spirit's influence, while, on the… | Of or pertaining to the Semi-Pelagians, or their tenets.
seedy: 1. Abounding with seeds; bearing seeds; having run to seeds. 2. Having a peculiar flavor supposed to be derived from the weeds growing among the vines; -- said of certain kinds of FRench brandy. 3. Old and worn out; exhausted; spiritless; also, poor and miserable looking; shabily clothed; shabby looking; as, he looked seedy coat. [Colloq.] Little Flanigan here . . .
selfposited: Disposed or arranged by an action originating in one's self or in itself. These molecular blocks of salt are self-posited. Tyndall.
segmentation: The act or process of dividing into segments; specifically (Biol.), a self-division into segments as a result of growth; cell cleavage; cell multiplication; endogenous cell formation. Segmentation cavity (Biol.), the cavity formed by the arrangement of the cells in segmentation or cleavage of the ovum; the cavity of the blastosphere.
seorita: A Spanish title of courtesy given to a young lady; Miss; also, a young lady.
seapig: (a) A porpoise or dolphin. (b) A dugong.
seafowl: Any bird which habitually frequents the sea, as an auk, gannet, gull, tern, or petrel; also, all such birds, collectively.
seedlop: A vessel in which a sower carries the seed to be scattered. [Prov. Eng.]
seawidgeon: (a) The scaup duck. (b) The pintail duck.
securely: In a secure manner; without fear or apprehension; without danger; safely. His daring foe . . . securely him defied. Milton.
sensated: Felt or apprehended through a sense, or the senses. Baxter.
selenate: A salt of selenic acid; -- formerly called also seleniate.
sepidaceous: Like or pertaining to the cuttlefishes of the genus Sepia.
seceder: 1. One who secedes. 2. (Eccl. Hist.) One of a numerous body of Presbyterians in Scotland who seceded from the communion of the Established Church, about the year 1733, and formed the Secession Church, so called.
selfdestructive: Destroying, or tending to destroy, one's self or itself; rucidal.
seducing: Seductive. "Thy sweet seducing charms." Cowper. -- Se*du"cing*ly, adv.
seld: Rare; uncommon; unusual. (old) Chaucer. Spenser. | Rarely; seldom. (old) Chaucer.
seriate: Arranged in a series or succession; pertaining to a series. -- Se"ri*ate*ly, adv.
sempervivum: A genus of fleshy-leaved plants, of which the houseleek (Sempervivum tectorum) is the commonest species.
serrous: Like the teeth off a saw; jagged. (old) Sir T. Browne.
sesquiduplicate: Twice and a half as great (as another thing); having the ratio of two and a half to one. Sesquiduplicate ratio (Math.), the ratio of two and a half to one, or one in which the greater term contains the lesser twice and a half, as that of 50 to 20.
secularness: The quality or state of being secular; worldliness; worldly- minded-ness.
seminifical: Forming or producing seed, or the male generative product of animals or of plants.
semioxygenated: Combined with oxygen only in part. Kirwan.
settle: 1. A seat of any kind. (old) "Upon the settle of his majesty" Hampole. 2. A bench; especially, a bench with a high back. 3. A place made lower than the rest; a wide step or platform lower than some… | 1. To place in a fixed or permanent condition; to make firm, steady, or stable; to establish; to fix; esp., to establish in life; to fix in business, in a home, or the like.
semiannular: Having the figure of a half circle; forming a semicircle. Grew.
selfopinioned: Having a high opinion of one's self; opinionated; conceited. South.
seismographic: Of or pertaining to a seismograph; indicated by a seismograph.
selaginella: A genus of cryptogamous plants resembling Lycopodia, but producing two kinds of spores; also, any plant of this genus. Many species are cultivated in conservatories.
seesaw: 1. A play among children in which they are seated upon the opposite ends of a plank which is balanced in the middle, and move alternately up and down. 2. A plank or board adjusted for this play. 3. | To move with a reciprocating motion; to move backward and forward, or upward and downward.
sere: [OE. seer, AS. seár (assumed) fr. seárian to wither; akin to D. zoor dry, LG. soor, OHG. soren to to wither, Gr. sush) to dry, to wither, Zend hush to dry. sq. root152. Cf. Austere, Sorrel, a.] Dry; | Dry; withered. Same as Sear. But with its sound it shook the sails That were so thin and sere. Coleridge.
sexradiate: Having six rays; -- said of certain sponge spicules. See Illust. of Spicule.
segmental: 1. Relating to, or being, a segment. 2. (Anat. & Zoöl.) (a) Of or pertaining to the segments of animals; as, a segmental duct; segmental papillæ. (b) Of or pertaining to the segmental organs. Segmental duct (Anat.), the primitive duct of the embryonic excretory organs which gives rise to the Wolffian duct and ureter; the pronephric duct. -- Segmental organs.
seid: A descendant of Mohammed through his daughter Fatima and nephew Ali.
semicalcareous: Half or partially calcareous; as, a semicalcareous plant.
sept: A clan, tribe, or family, proceeding from a common progenitor; -- used especially of the ancient clans in Ireland. The chief, struck by the illustration, asked at once to be baptized, and all his sept followed his example. S. Lover.
sepulture: 1. The act of depositing the dead body of a human being in the grave; burial; interment. Where we may royal sepulture prepare. Dryden. 2. A sepulcher; a grave; a place of burial. Drunkeness that the horrible sepulture of man's reason. Chaucer.
sesquipedal: Measuring or containing a foot and a half; as, a sesquipedalian pygmy; -- sometimes humorously applied to long words.
septuary: Something composed of seven; a week. Ash.
secco: Dry. Secco painting, or Painting in secco, painting on dry plaster, as distinguished from fresco painting, which is on wet or fresh plaster.
sensorial: Of or pertaining to the sensorium; as, sensorial faculties, motions, powers. A. Tucker.
sentencer: One who pronounced a sentence or condemnation.
sepoy: A native of India employed as a soldier in the service of a European power, esp. of Great Britain; an Oriental soldier disciplined in the European manner.
seafan: Any gorgonian which branches in a fanlike form, especially Gorgonia flabellum of Florida and the West Indies.
seedtime: The season proper for sowing. While the earth remaineth, seedtime and harvest, and cold and heat, and summer and winter, and day and night, shall not cease. Gen. viii. 22.
semeiotic: 1. Relating to signs or indications; pertaining to the language of signs, or to language generally as indicating thought. 2. (Med.) Of or pertaining to the signs or symptoms of diseases.
secondrate: Of the second size, rank, quality, or value; as, a second-rate ship; second-rate cloth; a second-rate champion. Dryden.
selenography: The science that treats of the physical features of the moon; - - corresponding to physical geography in respect to the earth. "Accurate selenography, or description of the moon." Sir T. Browne.
secureness: The condition or quality of being secure; exemption from fear; want of vigilance; security.
sextillion: According to the method of numeration (which is followed also in the United States), the number expressed by a unit with twenty-one ciphers annexed. According to the English method, a million raised to the sixth power, or the number expressed by a unit with thirty-six ciphers annexed. See Numeration.
sepalody: The metamorphosis of other floral organs into sepals or sepaloid bodies.
sesquitertian: Having the ratio of one and one third to one (as 4 : 3).
septennate: A period of seven years; as, the septennate during which the President of the French Republic holds office.
seapincushion: (a) A sea purse. (b) A pentagonal starfish.
selachian: One of the Selachii. See Illustration in Appendix.
semasiology: The science of meanings or sense development (of words); the explanation of the development and changes of the meanings of words. --Se*ma`si*o*log"ic*al (#), a.
seasoning: 1. The act or process by which anything is seasoned. 2. That which is added to any species of food, to give it a higher relish, as salt, spices, etc.; a condiment. 3. Hence, something added to enhance enjoyment or relieve dullness; as, wit is the seasoning of conversation.
seasickness: The peculiar sickness, characterized by nausea and prostration, which is caused by the pitching or rolling of a vessel.
separability: Quality of being separable or divisible; divisibility; separableness.
selfabuse: 1. The abuse of one's own self, powers, or faculties. 2. Self-deception; delusion. (old) Shak. 3. Masturbation; onanism; self-pollution.
selfcontradiction: The act of contradicting one's self or itself; repugnancy in conceptions or in terms; a proposition consisting of two members, one of which contradicts the other; as, to be and not to be at the same time is a self-contradiction.
setigerous: Covered with bristles; having or bearing a seta or setæ; setiferous; as, setigerous glands; a setigerous segment of an annelid; specifically (Bot.), tipped with a bristle.
seraph: One of an order of celestial beings, each having three pairs of wings. In ecclesiastical art and in poetry, a seraph is represented as one of a class of angels. Isa. vi. 2. As full, as perfect, in vile man that mourns, As the rapt seraph that adores and burns. Pope.
setiger: An annelid having setæ; a chætopod.
selfdelusion: The act of deluding one's self, or the state of being thus deluded.
setireme: A swimming leg (of an insect) having a fringe of hairs on the margin.
seventhirties: A name given to three several issues of United States Treasury notes, made during the Civil War, in denominations of $50 and over, bearing interest at the rate of seven and three tenths (thirty hundredths) per cent annually. Within a few years they were all redeemed or funded.
sephardim: Jews who are descendants of the former Jews of Spain and Portugal. They are as a rule darker than the northern Jews, and have more delicate features.
seduce: 1. To draw aside from the path of rectitude and duty in any manner; to entice to evil; to lead astray; to tempt and lead to iniquity; to corrupt. For me, the gold of France did not seduce. Shak. 2. Specifically, to induce to surrender chastity; to debauch by means of solicitation. Syn. -- To allure; entice; tempt; attract; mislead; decoy; inveigle. See Allure.
sediment: 1. The matter which subsides to the bottom, frrom water or any other liquid; settlings; lees; dregs. 2. (Geol.) The material of which sedimentary rocks are formed.
seedling: A plant reared from the seed, as distinguished from one propagated by layers, buds, or the like.
semaeostomata: A division of Discophora having large free mouth lobes. It includes Aurelia, and Pelagia. Called also Semeostoma. See Illustr. under Discophora, and Medusa.
selfaccused: Accused by one's self or by one's conscience. "Die self- accused." Cowper.
sepiostare: The bone or shell of cuttlefish. See Illust. under Cuttlefish.
semester: A period of six months; especially, a term in a college or uneversity which divides the year into two terms.
seamanship: The skill of a good seaman; the art, or skill in the art, of working a ship.
serviceable: 1. Doing service; promoting happiness, interest, advantage, or any good; useful to any end; adapted to any good end use; beneficial; advantageous. "Serviceable to religion and learning". Atterbury. "Serviceable tools." Macaulay. I know thee well, a serviceable villain. Shak. 2. Prepared for rendering service; capable of, or fit for, the performance of duty; hence, active;
semiplume: A feather which has a plumelike web, with the shaft of an ordinary feather.
senza: Without; as, senza stromenti, without instruments.
selfmoved: Moved by inherent power., without the aid of external impulse.
serrulation: 1. The state of being notched minutely, like a fine saw. Wright. 2. One of the teeth in a serrulate margin.
serenity: 1. The quality or state of being serene; clearness and calmness; quietness; stillness; peace. A general peace and serenity newly succeeded a general trouble. Sir W. Temple. 2. Calmness of mind; eveness of temper; undisturbed state; coolness; composure. I can not see how any men should ever transgress those moral rules with confidence and serenity. Locke.
selvagee: A skein or hank of rope yarns wound round with yarns or marline, -- used for stoppers, straps, etc.
serene: 1. Bright; clear; unabscured; as, a serene sky. The moon serene in glory mounts the sky. Pope. Full many a gem of purest ray serene The dark unfathomed caves of ocean bear. Gray. 2. Calm; placid; | 1. Serenity; clearness; calmness. [Poetic.] "The serene of heaven." Southey. To their master is denied To share their sweet serene. Young. 2. Etym: [F. serein evening dew or damp.
selfsuspicious: Suspicious or distrustful of one's self. Baxter.
seedsman: 1. A sower; one who sows or scatters seed. The seedsman Upon the slime and ooze scatters his grain. Shak. 2. A person who deals in seeds.
seafir: A sertularian hydroid, especially Sertularia abietina, which branches like a miniature fir tree.
selfevident: Evident without proof or reasoning; producing certainty or conviction upon a bare presentation to the mind; as, a self-evident proposition or truth. -- Self`-ev"i*dent*ly, adv.
selfrespect: Respect for one's self; regard for one's character; laudable self-esteem.
sesquialterate: Once and a half times as great as another; having the ratio of one and a half to one. Sesquialteral ratio (Math.), the ratio of one and a half to one; thus, 9 and 6 are in a sequialteral ratio.
septangle: A figure which has seven angles; a heptagon.
selfassured: Assured by or of one's self; self-reliant; complacent.
selfassumed: Assumed by one's own act, or without authority.
selfcontained: 1. Having self-control; reserved; uncommunicative; wholly engrossed in one's self. 2. (Mach.) Having all the essential working parts connected by a bedplate or framework, or contained in a case, etc., so that mutual relations of the parts do not depend upon fastening outside of the machine itself. Self-contained steam engine.
seljuckian: A member of the family of Seljuk; an adherent of that family, or subject of its government; (pl.) the dynasty of Turkish sultans sprung from Seljuk.
seclusive: Tending to seclude; keeping in seclusion; secluding; sequestering.
selfperplexed: Perplexed by doubts originating in one's own mind.
seafoam: 1. Foam of sea water. 2. (Min.) Meerschaum; -- called also sea froth.
sequoia: A genus of coniferous trees, consisting of two species, Sequoia Washingtoniana, syn. S. gigantea, the "big tree" of California, and S. sempervirens, the redwood, both of which attain an immense height.
seamat: Any bryozoan of the genus Flustra or allied genera which form frondlike corals.
september: The ninth month of the year, containing thurty days.
sepulchre: The place in which the dead body of a human being is interred, or a place set apart for that purpose; a grave; a tomb. The stony entrance of this sepulcher. Shak. | To bury; to inter; to entomb; as, obscurely sepulchered. And so sepulchered in such pomp dost lie That kings for such a tomb would wish to die. Milton.
seaear: Any species of ear-shaped shells of the genus Haliotis. See Abalone.
semidetached: Half detached; partly distinct or separate. Semidetached house, one of two tenements under a single roof, but separated by a party wall. [Eng.]
sekes: A place in a pagan temple in which the images of the deities were inclosed.
seduction: 1. The act of seducing; enticement to wrong doing; specifically, the offense of inducing a woman to consent to unlawful sexual intercourse, by enticements which overcome her scruples; the wrong or crime of persuading a woman to surrender her chastity. 2. That which seduces, or is adapted to seduce; means of leading astray; as, the seductions of wealth.
selfbinder: A reaping machine containing mechanism for binding the grain into sheaves.
semiproof: Half proof; evidence from the testimony of a single witness. (old) Bailey.
sectiuncle: A little or petty sect. "Some new sect or sectiuncle." J. Martineau.
selfactivity: The quality or state of being self-active; self-action.
seaduck: Any one of numerous species of ducks which frequent the seacoasts and feed mainly on fishes and mollusks. The scoters, eiders, old squaw, and ruddy duck are examples. They may be distinguished by the lobate hind toe.
segment: 1. One of the parts into which any body naturally separates or is divided; a part divided or cut off; a section; a portion; as, a segment of an orange; a segment of a compound or divided leaf. 2. | To divide or separate into parts in growth; to undergo segmentation, or cleavage, as in the segmentation of the ovum.
seascorpion: (a) A European sculpin (Cottus scorpius) having the head armed with short spines. (b) The scorpene.
semiquartile: An aspect of the planets when distant from each other the half of a quadrant, or forty-five degrees, or one sign and a half. Hutton.
settee: A long seat with a back, -- made to accommodate several persons at once. | A vessel with a very long, sharp prow, carrying two or three masts with lateen sails, -- used in the Mediterranean. [Written also setee.]
selfpropagating: Propagating by one's self or by itself.
seawan: The name used by the Algonquin Indians for the shell beads which passed among the Indians as money. Note: Seawan was of two kinds; wampum, white, and suckanhock, black or purple, -- the former having half the value of the latter. Many writers, however, use the terms seawan and wampum indiscriminately. Bartlett.
selah: A word of doubtful meaning, occuring frequently in the Psalms; by some, supposed to signify silence or a pause in the musical performance of the song. Beyond the fact that Selach is a musical term, we know absolutely nothing about it. Dr. W. Smith (Bib. Dict.)
semisextile: An aspect of the planets when they are distant from each other the twelfth part of a circle, or thirty degrees. Hutton.
seapool: A pool of salt water. Spenser.
servomotor: A relay apparatus; specif.: (a) An auxiliary motor, regulated by a hand lever, for quickly and easily moving the reversing gear of a large marine engine into any desired position indicated by that of the hand lever, which controls the valve of the motor. (b) In a Whitehead torpedo, a compressed-air motor, for moving the rudders so as to correct deviations from the course.
searobin: See under Robin, and Illustration in Appendix.
sedimentary: Of or pertaining to sediment; formed by sediment; containing matter that has subsided. Sedimentary rocks. (Geol.) See Aqueous rocks, under Aqueous.
seepy: Oozy; -- applied to land under cultivation that is not well drained.
senecas: A tribe of Indians who formerly inhabited a part of Western New York. This tribe was the most numerous and most warlike of the Five Nations. Seneca grass(Bot.), holy grass. See under Holy. -- Seneca eil, petroleum or naphtha. -- Seneca root, or Seneca snakeroot (Bot.), the rootstock of an American species of milkworth (Polygala Senega) having an aromatic but bitter taste.
seckel: A small reddish brown sweet and juicy pear. It originated on a farm near Philadelphia, afterwards owned by a Mr. Seckel.
sesquialteral: Once and a half times as great as another; having the ratio of one and a half to one. Sesquialteral ratio (Math.), the ratio of one and a half to one; thus, 9 and 6 are in a sequialteral ratio.
seapass: A document carried by neutral merchant vessels in time of war, to show their nationality; a sea letter or passport. See Passport.
secretory: Secreting; performing, or connected with, the office secretion; secernent; as, secretory vessels, nerves. -- n. A secretory vessel; a secernent.
seaslater: Any isopod crustacean of the genus Ligia.
sedimentation: The act of depositing a sediment; specifically (Geol.), the deposition of the material of which sedimentary rocks are formed.
serf: A servant or slave employed in husbandry, and in some countries attached to the soil and transferred with it, as formerly in Russia. In England, at least from the reign of Henry II, one only, and that the inferior species [of villeins], existed . . .
sevennight: A week; any period of seven consecutive days and nights. See Sennight.
seposit: To set aside; to give up. (old)
servient: Subordinate. [Obs. except in law.] Dyer. Servient tenement or estate (Law), that on which the burden of a servitude or an easement is imposed. Cf. Dominant estate, under Dominant. Gale & Whately.
semibull: A bull issued by a pope in the period between his election and coronation.
seminarist: A member of, or one educated in, a seminary; specifically, an ecclesiastic educated for the priesthood in a seminary.
several: 1. Separate; distinct; particular; single. Each several ship a victory did gain. Dryden. Each might his several province well command, Would all but stoop to what they understand. Pope. 2. Diverse; | By itself; severally. (old) Every kind of thing is laid up several in barns or storehoudses. Robynson (More's Utopia).
sewel: A scarecrow, generally made of feathers tied to a string, hung up to prevent deer from breaking into a place. Halliwell.
seatang: A kind of seaweed; tang; tangle. To their nests of sedge and sea tang. Longfellow.
serosity: 1. The quality or state of being serous. 2. (Physiol.) A thin watery animal fluid, as synovial fluid and pericardial fluid.
selfregulative: Tending or serving to regulate one's self or itself. Whewell.
sepulchral: 1. Of or pertaining to burial, to the grave, or to monuments erected to the memory of the dead; as, a sepulchral stone; a sepulchral inscription. 2. Unnaturally low and grave; hollow in tone; -- said of sound, especially of the voice. This exaggerated dulling of the voice . . . giving what is commonly called a sepulchral tone. H. Sweet.
search: 1. To look over or through, for the purpose of finding something; to examine; to explore; as, to search the city. "Search the Scriptures." John v. 39. They are come to search the house. Shak. | To seek; to look for something; to make inquiry, exploration, or examination; to hunt. Once more search with me. Shak. It sufficeth that they have once with care sifted the matter, and searched into…
septum: 1. A wall separating two cavities; a partition; as, the nasal septum. 2. (Bot.) A partition that separates the cells of a fruit. 3. (Zoöl.) (a) One of the radial calcareous plates of a coral. (b) One of the transverse partitions dividing the shell of a mollusk, or of a rhizopod, into several chambers. See Illust. under Nautilus.
septiform: Having the form of a septum.
seaporcupine: Any fish of the genus Diodon, and allied genera, whose body is covered with spines. See Illust. under Diodon.
separative: Causing, or being to cause, separation. "Separative virtue of extreme cold." Boyle.
senhorita: A Spanish title of courtesy given to a young lady; Miss; also, a young lady.
secale: A genus of cereal grasses including rye.
selfconjugate: Having the two things that are conjugate parts of the same figure; as, self-conjugate triangles.
selfabased: Humbled by consciousness of inferiority, unworthiness, guilt, or shame.
selfacting: Acting of or by one's self or by itself; -- said especially of a machine or mechanism which is made to perform of or for itself what is usually done by human agency; automatic; as, a self-acting feed apparatus; a self-acting mule; a self-acting press.
seirospore: One of several spores arranged in a chain as in certain algæ of the genus Callithamnion.
seawillow: A gorgonian coral with long flexible branches.
separatistic: Of or pertaining to separatists; characterizing separatists; schismatical.
serpigo: A dry, scaly eruption on the skin; especially, a ringworm.
sensory: Of or pertaining to the sensorium or sensation; as, sensory impulses; -- especially applied to those nerves and nerve fibers which convey to a nerve center impulses resulting in sensation; also sometimes loosely employed in the sense of afferent, to indicate nerve fibers which convey impressions of any kind to a nerve center.
seacorn: A yellow cylindrical mass of egg capsule of certain species of whelks (Buccinum), which resembles an ear of maize.
sentry: 1. (Mil.) A soldier placed on guard; a sentinel. 2. Guard; watch, as by a sentinel. Here toils, and death, and death's half-brother, sleep, Forms terrible to view, their sentry keep. Dryden. Sentry box, a small house or box to cover a sentinel at his post, and shelter him from the weather.
sevenup: The game of cards called also all fours, and old sledge. [U. S.]
seriality: The quality or state of succession in a series; sequence. H. Spenser.
seel: 1. (Falconry) To close the eyes of (a hawk or other bird) by drawing through the lids threads which were fastened over the head. Bacon. Fools climbs to fall: fond hopes, like seeled doves for want of… | To incline to one side; to lean; to roll, as a ship at sea. (old) Sir W. Raleigh.
selfcolor: A color not mixed or variegated.
self: Same; particular; very; identical. [Obs., except in the compound selfsame.] "On these self hills." Sir. W. Raleigh. To shoot another arrow that self way Which you did shoot the first. Shak. | 1. The individual as the object of his own reflective consciousness; the man viewed by his own cognition as the subject of all his mental phenomena, the agent in his own activities, the subject of…
selfdeceived: Deceived or misled respecting one's self by one's own mistake or error.
sergeancy: The office of a sergeant; sergeantship. [Written also serjeancy.]
seapoppy: The horn poppy. See under Horn.
serpentinize: To convert (a magnesian silicate) into serpentine. -- Ser`pen*tin`i*za"tion, n.
selfsacrificing: Yielding up one's own interest, ffeelings, etc; sacrificing one's self.
selfmoving: Moving by inherent power, without the aid of external impulse.
sermon: 1. A discourse or address; a talk; a writing; as, the sermens of Chaucer. (old) Chaucer. 2. Specifically, a discourse delivered in public, usually by a clergyman, for the purpose of religious… | To speak; to discourse; to compose or deliver a sermon. (old) Holinshed. What needeth it to sermon of it more Chaucer.
sessileeyed: Having eyes which are not elevated on a stalk; -- opposed to stalk-eyed. Sessile-eyed Crustacea, the Arthrostraca.
sententiarist: A sententiary. Barnas Sears (Life of Luther).
senectitude: Old age. "Senectitude, weary of its toils." H. Miller.
seafaring: Following the business of a mariner; as, a seafaring man.
selenitic: Of or pertaining to selenite; resembling or containing selenite.
seventyfour: A naval vessel carrying seventy-four guns.
septemfluous: Flowing sevenfold; divided into seven streams or currents. Fuller.
seacoast: The shore or border of the land adjacent to the sea or ocean. Also used adjectively.
selflove: The love of one's self; desire of personal happiness; tendency to seek one's own benefit or advantage. Shak. Self-love, the spring of motion, acts the soul. Pope. Syn. -- Selfishness. -- Self-love, Selfishness. The term self-love is used in a twofold sense: 1.
sensificatory: Susceptible of, or converting into, sensation; as, the sensificatory part of a nervous system. Huxley.
selfculture: Culture, training, or education of one's self by one's own efforts.
seismometric: Of or pertaining to seismometry, or seismometer; as, seismometric instruments; seismometric measurements.
sequacious: 1. Inclined to follow a leader; following; attendant. Trees uprooted left their place, Sequacious of the lyre. Dryden. 2. Hence, ductile; malleable; pliant; manageable. semiangle: The half of a given, or measuring, angle.
servility: The quality or state of being servile; servileness. To be a queen in bondage is more vile Than is a slave in base servility. Shak.

septembrist: An agent in the massacres in Paris, committed in patriotic frenzy, on the 22d of September, 1792.

sesquialter: A stop on the organ, containing several ranks of pipes which reënforce some of the high harmonics of the ground tone, and make the sound more brilliant.

seriation: Arrangement or position in a series.
seamilkwort: A low, fleshy perennial herb (Glaux maritima) found along northern seashores.
semitonic: Of or pertaining to a semitone; consisting of a semitone, or of semitones.

senatorship: The office or dignity of a senator. Carew.
seagherkin: Any small holothurian resembling in form a gherkin.
selfopinion: Opinion, especially high opinion, of one's self; an overweening estimate of one's self or of one's own opinion. Collier.
seeksorrow: One who contrives to give himself vexation. [Archaic.] Sir P. Sidney.
seminist: A believer in the old theory that the newly created being is formed by the admixture of the seed of the male with the supposed seed of the female.
serumtherapy: The treatment of disease by the injection of blood serum from immune animals.
serenely: 1. In a serene manner; clearly. Now setting Phoebus shone serenely bright. Pope. 2. With unruffled temper; coolly; calmly. Prior.
semivitrification: 1. The quality or state of being semivitrified. 2. A substance imperfectly vitrified.

sematology: The doctrine of signs as the expression of thought or reasoning; the science of indicating thought by signs. Smart.
selfconfidence: The quality or state of being self-confident; self-reliance. A feeling of self-confidence which supported and sustained him. Beaconsfield.
selfrepelling: Made up of parts, as molecules or atoms, which mutually repel each other; as, gases are self-repelling.

selfsufficing: Sufficing for one's self or for itself, without needing external aid; self-sufficient. -- Self`-suf*fi"cing*ness, n. J. C. Shairp.
seerhand: A kind of muslin of a texture between nainsook and mull.
secretomotory: Causing secretion; -- said of nerves which go to glands and influence secretion.
seer: Sore; painful. [Prov. Eng.] Ray. | A person who foresees events; a prophet. Milton.
setwall: A plant formerly valued for its restorative qualities (Valeriana officinalis, or V. Pyrenaica). (old) [Written also setwal.] Chaucer.
sectility: The state or quality of being sectile.

semibarbarian: Half barbarous; partially civilized. -- n. One partly civilized.
selenite: A variety of gypsum, occuring in transparent crystals or crystalline masses.

sedation: The act of calming, or the state of being calm. Coles.

selfjustifier: One who excuses or justifies himself. J. M. Mason.

serpette: A pruning knife with a curved blade. Knight.

sensist: One who, in philosophy, holds to sensism.

septuagesima: The third Sunday before Lent; -- so called because it is about seventy days before Easter.

separatical: Of or pertaining to separatism in religion; schismatical. Dr. T. Dwight.
seatoad: (a) A sculpin. (b) A toadfish. (c) The angler.

seawhip: A gorgonian having a simple stem.

serration: 1. Condition of being serrate; formation in the shape of a saw. 2. One of the teeth in a serrate or serrulate margin.

sell: Self. [Obs. or Scot.] B. Jonson. | A cell; a house. (old) Chaucer.

seeder: One who, or that which, sows or plants seed.
sectator: A follower; a disciple; an adherent to a sect. (old) Sir W. Raleigh.

seigniorize: To lord it over. (old) As proud as he that seigniorizeth hell. Fairfax.
selfexaltation: The act of exalting one's self, or the state of being so exalted.

seagreen: Of a beautiful bluish green color, like sea water on soundings.

severable: Capable of being severed. Encyc. Dict.

sexifid: Six-cleft; as, a sexfid calyx or nectary.

seignior: 1. A lord; the lord of a manor. 2. A title of honor or of address in the South of Europe, corresponding to Sir or Mr. in English. Grand Seignior, the sultan of Turkey.
selterswater: A mineral water from Sellers, in the district of Nassan, Germany, containing much free carbonic acid.
serieswinding: A winding in which the armature coil and the field-magnet coil are in series with the external circuits; -- opposed to shunt winding. --Se"ries-wound`, a.
seashell: The shell of any marine mollusk.
seasalmon: (a) A young pollock. (b) The spotted squeteague. (c) See Sea bass (b).
selfdevouring: Devouring one's self or itself. Danham.
senora: A Spanish title of courtesy given to a lady; Mrs.; Madam; also, a lady.
seadove: The little auk, or rotche. See Illust. of Rotche.
sensualistic: 1. Sensual. 2. Adopting or teaching the doctrines of sensualism.
seahorse: 1. A fabulous creature, half horse and half fish, represented in classic mythology as driven by sea dogs or ridden by the Nereids. It is also depicted in heraldry. See Hippocampus. 2. (Zoöl.) (a) The walrus. (b) Any fish of the genus Hippocampus. Note: In a passage of Dryden's, the word is supposed to refer to the hippopotamus.
selfmettle: Inborn mettle or courage; one's own temper. (old) Shak.
selfconsidering: Considering in one's own mind; deliberating. Pope.
selfcolored: Being of a single color; -- applied to flowers, animals, and textile fabrics.
sensation: 1. (Physiol.) An impression, or the consciousness of an impression, made upon the central nervous organ, through the medium of a sensory or afferent nerve or one of the organs of sense; a feeling, or state of consciousness, whether agreeable or disagreeable, produced either by an external object (stimulus), or by some change in the internal state of the body.
seigniorage: 1. Something claimed or taken by virtue of sovereign prerogative; specifically, a charge or toll deducted from bullion brought to a mint to be coined; the difference between the cost of a mass of bullion and the value as money of the pieces coined from it.
sentine: A place for dregs and dirt; a sink; a sewer. (old) Latimer.
senseless: Destitute of, deficient in, or contrary to, sense; without sensibility or feeling; unconscious; stupid; foolish; unwise; unreasonable. You blocks, you stones, you worse than senseless things. Shak. The ears are senseless that should give us hearing. Shak. The senseless grave feels not your pious sorrows. Rowe. They were a senseless, stupid race. Swift.
selfglorious: Springing from vainglory or vanity; vain; boastful. Dryden.
select: Taken from a number by preferance; picked out as more valuable or exellent than others; of special value or exellence; nicely chosen; selected; choice. A few select spirits had separated from the… | To choose and take from a number; to take by preference from among others; to pick out; to cull; as, to select the best authors for perusal. "One peculiar nation to select." Milton. The pious chief .
sesquipedalian: Measuring or containing a foot and a half; as, a sesquipedalian pygmy; -- sometimes humorously applied to long words.
selfluminous: Possessing in itself the property of emitting light. Sir D. Brewster.
semimute: Having the faculty of speech but imperfectly developed or partially lost.
sesquioxide: An oxide containing three atoms of oxygen with two atoms (or radicals) of some other substance; thus, alumina, Al2O3 is a sesquioxide.
semisoun: A half sound; a low tone. (old) "Soft he cougheth with a semisoun." Chaucer.
semideistical: Half deisticsl; bordering on deism. S. Miller.
serfdom: The state or condition of a serf.
selfconviction: The act of convicting one's self, or the state of being self- convicted.
semen: 1. (Bot.) The seed of plants. 2. (Physiol.) The seed or fecundating fluid of male animals; sperm. It is a white or whitish viscid fluid secreted by the testes, characterized by the presence of spermatozoids to which it owes its generative power.
selfexcite: To energize or excite (the field magnets of a dynamo) by induction from the residual magnetism of its cores, leading all or a part of the current thus produced through the field-magnet coils.
semipellucid: Half clear, or imperfectly transparent; as, a semipellucid gem.
searching: Exploring thoroughly; scrutinizing; penetrating; trying; as, a searching discourse; a searching eye. "Piercing, searching, biting, cold." Dickens. -- Search"ing*ly, adv. -- Search"ing*ness, n.
septillion: According to the French method of numeration (which is followed also in the United States), the number expressed by a unit with twenty-four ciphers annexed. According to the English method, the number expressed by a unit with forty-two ciphers annexed. See Numeration.
semiquaver: A note of half the duration of the quaver; -- now usually called a sixsteenth note.
selfinduction: Induction in a circuit due to the action of one portion of a current upon an adjacent portion during periods of varying current strength. The nature of the induction is such as to oppose the action which produces it.
searaven: (a) An American cottoid fish (Hemitripterus Americanus) allied to the sculpins, found on the northeren Atlantic coasts. (b) The cormorant.
sesban: A leguminous shrub (Sesbania aculeata) which furnishes a fiber used for making ropes. Note: The name is applied also to the similar plant, Sesbania Ægyptiaca, and other species of the same genus.
semifable: That which is part fable and part truth; a mixture of truth and fable. De Quincey.
sensibility: 1. (Physiol.) The quality or state of being sensible, or capable of sensation; capacity to feel or perceive. 2. The capacity of emotion or feeling, as distinguished from the intellect and the will; peculiar susceptibility of impression, pleasurable or painful; delicacy of feeling; quick emotion or sympathy; as, sensibility to pleasure or pain; sensibility to shame or praise;
selfdevotion: The act of devoting one's self, or the state of being self- devoted; willingness to sacrifice one's own advantage or happiness for the sake of others; self-sacrifice.
selfhood: Existence as a separate self, or independent person; conscious personality; individuality. Bib. Sacra.
semicircular: Having the form of half of a circle. Addison. Semicircular canals (Anat.), certain canals of the inner ear. See under Ear.
selfhelp: The act of aiding one's self, without depending on the aid of others.
sealeopard: Any one of several species of spotted seals, especially Ogmorhinus leptonyx, and Leptonychotes Weddelli, of the Antarctic Ocean. The North Pacific sea leopard is the harbor seal.
sentiment: 1. A thought prompted by passion or feeling; a state of mind in view of some subject; feeling toward or respecting some person or thing; disposition prompting to action or expression.
sesquisalt: A salt derived from a sesquioxide base, or made up on the proportions of a sesqui compound.
sertularia: A genus of delicate branching hydroids having small sessile hydrothecæ along the sides of the branches.
setter: 1. One who, or that which, sets; -- used mostly in composition with a noun, as typesetter; or in combination with an adverb, as a setter on (or inciter), a setter up, a setter forth. 2. | To cut the dewlap (of a cow or an ox), and to insert a seton, so as to cause an issue. [Prov. Eng.]
setto: A contest in boxing, in an argument, or the like. [Colloq.] Halliwell.
semicirque: A semicircular hollow or opening among trees or hills. Wordsworth.
seemliness: The quality or state of being seemly: comeliness; propriety.
semined: Thickly covered or sown, as with seeds. (old) B. Jonson.
seclusion: The act of secluding, or the state of being secluded; separation from society or connection; a withdrawing; privacy; as, to live in seclusion. O blest seclusion from a jarring world, which he, thus occupied, enjoys! Cowper. Syn. -- Solitude; separation; withdrawment; retirement; privacy. See Solitude.
seapork: An American compound ascidian (Amoræcium stellatum) which forms large whitish masses resembling salt pork.
servicehat: A cap or hat worn by officers or enlisted men when full-dress uniform, or dress uniform, is not worn. In the United States army the service cap is round, about 3½ inches high, flat-topped, with a visor. The service hat is of soft felt of khaki color, with broad brim and high crown, creased down the middle.
sextans: 1. (Rom. Antiq.) A Roman coin, the sixth part of an as. 2. (Astron.) A constellation on the equator south of Leo; the Sextant.
seen: Versed; skilled; accomplished. (old) Well seen in every science that mote be. Spenser. Noble Boyle, not less in nature seen, Than his great brother read in states and men. Dryden.
seasoner: One who, or that which, seasons, or gives a relish; a seasoning.
septilateral: Having seven sides; as, a septilateral figure.
semidiurnal: 1. Pertaining to, or accomplished in, half a day, or twelve hours; occurring twice every day. 2. Pertaining to, or traversed in, six hours, or in half the time between the rising and setting of a heavenly body; as, a semidiurnal arc.
senhor: A Spanish title of courtesy corresponding to the English Mr. or Sir; also, a gentleman.
sexenary: Proceeding by sixes; sextuple; -- applied especially to a system of arithmetical computation in which the base is six.
seagirkin: Any small holothurian resembling in form a gherkin.
sermocinator: One who makes sermons or speeches. (old) Howell.
selfpositing: The act of disposing or arranging one's self or itself. The self-positing of the molecules. R. Watts.
seam: Grease; tallow; lard. [Obs. or prov. Eng.] Shak. Dryden. | 1. The fold or line formed by sewing together two pieces of cloth or leather. 2. Hence, a line of junction; a joint; a suture, as on a ship, a floor, or other structure;
semivocal: Of or pertaining to a semivowel; half cocal; imperfectly sounding.
semirecondite: Half hidden or half covered; said of the head of an insect when half covered by the shield of the thorax.
selfaffrighted: Frightened at or by one's self. Shak.
separatist: One who withdraws or separates himself; especially, one who withdraws from a church to which he has belonged; a seceder from an established church; a dissenter; a nonconformist; a schismatic; a sectary. Heavy fines on divines who should preach in any meeting of separatist . Macaulay.
sector: 1. (Geom.) A part of a circle comprehended between two radii and the included arc. 2. A mathematical instrument, consisting of two rulers connected at one end by a joint, each arm marked with several scales, as of equal parts, chords, sines, tangents, etc., one scale of each kind on each arm, and all on lines radiating from the common center of motion.
semipalmate: Having the anterior toes joined only part way down with a web; half-webbed; as, a semipalmate bird or foot. See Illust. k under Aves.
selfrestrained: Restrained by one's self or itself; restrained by one's own power or will.
semilenticular: Half lenticular or convex; imperfectly resembling a lens. Kirwan.
selfsatisfied: Satisfied with one's self or one's actions; self-complacent.
setterwort: The bear's-foot (Helleborus foetidus); -- so called because the root was used in settering, or inserting setons into the dewlaps of cattle. Called also pegroots. Dr. Prior.
selfconceit: Conceit of one's self; an overweening opinion of one's powers or endowments. Syn. -- See Egotism.
secund: Arranged on one side only, as flowers or leaves on a stalk. Gray.
separating: Designed or employed to separate. Separating funnel (Chem.), a funnel, often globe-shaped, provided with a stopcock for the separate drawing off of immiscible liquids of different specific gravities.
sealetter: The customary certificate of national character which neutral merchant vessels are bound to carry in time of war; a passport for a vessel and cargo.
seafeather: Any gorgonian which branches in a plumelike form.
seasaurian: Any marine saurian; esp. (Paleon.) the large extinct species of Mosasaurus, Icthyosaurus, Plesiosaurus, and related genera.
sentiency: The quality or state of being sentient; esp., the quality or state of having sensation. G. H. Lewes An example of harmonious action between the intelligence and the sentieny of the mind. Earle.
senate: 1. An assembly or council having the highest deliberative and legislative functions. Specifically: (a) (Anc. Rom.) A body of elders appointed or elected from among the nobles of the nation, and having supreme legislative authority. The senate was thus the medium through which all affairs of the whole government had to pass. Dr. W. Smith.
septinsular: Consisting of seven islands; as, the septinsular republic of the Ionian Isles.
seppuku: Same as Hara-kiri. Seppuku, or hara-kiri, also came into vogue. W. E. Griffis.
sequestrable: Capable of being sequestered; subject or liable to sequestration.
sennight: The space of seven nights and days; a week. [Written also se'nnight.] [Archaic.] Shak. Tennyson.
seachart: A chart or map on which the lines of the shore, islands, shoals, harbors, etc., are delineated.
septentrionate: To tend or point toward the north; to north. Sir T. Browne.
seek: 1. To go in search of; to look for; to search for; to try to find. The man saked him, saying, What seekest thou And he said, I seek my brethren. Gen. xxxvii. 15,16. 2. To inquire for; to ask for; | To make search or inquiry: to endeavor to make discovery. Seek ye out of the book of the Lord, and read. Isa. xxxiv. 16. To seek, needing to seek or search; hence, unpreparated.
senator: 1. A member of a senate. The duke and senators of Venice greet you. Shak. Note: In the United States, each State sends two senators for a term of six years to the national Congress. 2. (O.Eng.Law) A member of the king's council; a king's councilor. Burrill.
seabuilt: Built at, in, or by the sea.
selfexplaining: Explaining itself; capable of being understood without explanation.
serigraph: An autographic device to test the strength of raw silk.
secondhand: 1. Not original or primary; received from another. They have but a secondhand or implicit knowledge. Locke. 2. Not new; already or previously or used by another; as, a secondhand book, garment. At second hand. See Hand, n., 10.
sericeous: 1. Of or pertaining to silk; consisting of silk; silky. 2. (Bot.) Covered with very soft hairs pressed close to the surface; as, a sericeous leaf. 3. (Zoöl.) Having a silklike luster, usually due to fine, close hairs.
serac: A pinnacle of ice among the crevasses of a glacier; also, one of the blocks into which a glacier breaks on a steep grade.
secessionism: The doctrine or policy of secession; the tenets of secession; the tenets of secessionists.
selffertilization: The fertilization of a flower by pollen from the same flower and without outer aid; autogamy.
sexfid: Six-cleft; as, a sexfid calyx or nectary.
serpenttongued: Having a forked tongue, like a serpent.
semilogical: Half logical; partly logical; said of fallacies. Whately.
secrete: 1. To deposit in a place of hiding; to hide; to conceal; as, to secrete stolen goods; to secrete one's self. 2. (Physiol.) To separate from the blood and elaborate by the process of secretion; to elaborate and emit as a secretion. See Secretion. Why one set of cells should secrete bile, another urea, and so on, we do not known. Carpenter. Syn. -- To conceal; hide. See Conceal.
semeiological: Of or pertaining to the science of signs, or the systematic use of signs; as, a semeiological classification of the signs or symptoms of disease; a semeiological arrangement of signs used as signals.
seahare: Any tectibranchiate mollusk of the genus Aplysia. See Aplysia.
seabeast: Any large marine mammal, as a seal, walrus, or cetacean.
selfwrong: Wrong done by a person himself. Shak.
sepiment: Something that separates; a hedge; a fence. Bailey.
sennit: 1. (Naut.) A braided cord or fabric formed by plaiting together rope yarns or other small stuff. 2. Plaited straw or palm leaves for making hats.
sextolet: A double triplet; a group of six equal notes played in the time of four.
semicastrate: To deprive of one testicle. -- Sem`i*cas*tra"tion,n.
section: 1. The act of cutting, or separation by cutting; as, the section of bodies. 2. A part separated from something; a division; a portion; a slice. Specifically: -- (a) A distinct part or portion of a book or writing; a subdivision of a chapter; the division of a law or other writing; a paragraph; an article; hence, the character §, often used to denote such a division.
seapartridge: The gilthead (Crenilabrus melops), a fish of the British coasts.
secession: 1. The act of seceding; separation from fellowship or association with others, as in a religious or political organization; withdrawal. 2. (U.S. Hist.) The withdrawal of a State from the national Union. Secession Church (in Scotland). See Seceder.
sexagesimal: Pertaining to, or founded on, the number sixty. Sexagesimal fractions or numbers (Arith. & Alg.), those fractions whose denominators are some power of sixty; as, astronomical fractions, because formerly there were no others used in astronomical calculations. -- Sexagesimal, or Sexagenary, arithmetic, the method of computing by the sexagenary scale, or by sixties.
septfoil: 1. (Bot.) A European herb, the tormentil. See Tormentil. 2. (Arch.) An ornamental foliation having seven lobes. Cf. Cinquefoil, Quarterfoil, and Trefoil. 3. (Eccl.Art.) A typical figure, consisting of seven equal segments of a circle, used to denote the gifts of the Holy Chost, the seven sacraments as recognized by the Roman Catholic Church, etc.
seamark: Any elevated object on land which serves as a guide to mariners; a beacon; a landmark visible from the sea, as a hill, a tree, a steeple, or the like. Shak.
sexton: An under officer of a church, whose business is to take care of the church building and the vessels, vestments, etc., belonging to the church, to attend on the officiating clergyman, and to perform other duties pertaining to the church, such as to dig graves, ring the bell, etc. Sexton beetle (Zoöl.), a burying beetle.
semiditone: A lesser third, having its terms as 6 to 5; a hemiditone.
seraphical: Of or pertaining to a seraph; becoming, or suitable to, a seraph; angelic; sublime; pure; refined. "Seraphic arms and trophies." Milton. "Seraphical fervor." Jer. Taylor. -- Se*raph"ic*al*ly, adv. -- Se*raph"ic*al*ness, n.
sensibleness: 1. The quality or state of being sensible; sensibility; appreciation; capacity of perception; susceptibility. "The sensibleness of the eye." Sharp. "Sensibleness and sorrow for sin." Hammond. The sensibleness of the divine presence. Hallywell. 2. Intelligence; reasonableness; good sense.
sermonize: 1. To compose or write a sermon or sermons; to preach. 2. To inculcate rigid rules. Chesterfield. | To preach or discourse to; to affect or influence by means of a sermon or of sermons. Which of us shall sing or sermonize the other fast asleep Landor.
sensitive: 1. Having sense of feeling; possessing or exhibiting the capacity of receiving impressions from external objects; as, a sensitive soul. 2. Having quick and acute sensibility, either to the action of external objects, or to impressions upon the mind and feelings; highly susceptible; easily and acutely affected. She was too sensitive to abuse and calumny. Macaulay. 3.
sebacic: Of or pertaining to fat; derived from, or resembling, fat; specifically, designating an acid (formerly called also sebic, and pyroleic, acid), obtained by the distillation or saponification of certain oils (as castor oil) as a white crystalline substance.
sess: To lay a tax upon; to assess. (old) | A tax; an assessment. See Cess. (old)
semihistorical: Half or party historical. Sir G. C. Lewis.
semeiography: A description of the signs of disease.
seabird: Any swimming bird frequenting the sea; a sea fowl.
serum: (a) The watery portion of certain animal fluids, as blood, milk, etc. (b) A thin watery fluid, containing more or less albumin, secreted by the serous membranes of the body, such as the pericardium and peritoneum. Blood serum, the pale yellowish fluid which exudes from the clot formed in the coagulation of the blood;
secern: 1. To separate; to distinguish. Averroes secerns a sense of titillation, and a sense of hunger and thirst. Sir W. Hamilton. 2. (Physiol.) To secrete; as, mucus secerned in the nose. Arbuthnot.
secondarily: 1. In a secondary manner or degree. 2. Secondly; in the second place. (old) God hath set some in the church, first apostels, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers. 1 Cor. xii. 28.
sectary: A sectarian; a member or adherent of a sect; a follower or disciple of some particular teacher in philosophy or religion; one who separates from an established church; a dissenter. I never knew that time in England when men of truest religion were not counted sectaries. Milton.
secretness: 1. The state or quality of being secret, hid, or concealed. 2. Secretiveness; concealment. Donne.
sextant: 1. (Math.) The sixth part of a circle. 2. An instrument for measuring angular distances between objects, -- used esp. at sea, for ascertaining the latitude and longitude. It is constructed on the same optical principle as Hadley's quadrant, but usually of metal, with a nicer graduation, telescopic sight, and its arc the sixth, and sometimes the third, part of a circle.
semisavage: Half savage. | One who is half savage.
seminymph: The pupa of insects which undergo only a slight change in passing to the imago state.
semidiapente: An imperfect or diminished fifth. Busby.
selfview: A view if one's self; specifically, carefulness or regard for one's own interests
seamouse: (a) A dorsibranchiate annelid, belonging to Aphrodite and allied genera, having long, slender, hairlike setæ on the sides. (b) The dunlin.
semiform: A half form; an imperfect form.
secretservice: The detective service of a government. In the United States, in time of peace the bureau of secret service is under the treasury department, and in time of war it aids the war department in securing information concerning the movements of the enemy.
selfstarter: A mechanism (usually one operated by electricity, compressed air, a spring, or an explosive gas), attached to an internal- combustion engine, as on an automobile, and used as a means of starting the engine without cranking it by hand.
selfapproving: Approving one's own action or character by one's own judgment. One self-approving hour whole years outweighs Of stupid starers and of loud huzzas. Pope.
selfconscious: 1. Conscious of one's acts or state as belonging to, or originating in, one's self. "My self-conscious worth." Dryden. 2. Conscious of one's self as an object of the observation of others; as, the speaker was too self-conscious.
sebiferous: 1. (Bot.) Producing vegetable tallow. 2. (Physiol.) Producing fat; sebaceous; as, the sebiferous, or sebaceous, glands.
sensationalist: 1. (Metaph.) An advocate of, or believer in, philosophical sensationalism. 2. One who practices sensational writing or speaking.
seminarian: A member of, or one educated in, a seminary; specifically, an ecclesiastic educated for the priesthood in a seminary.
security: 1. The condition or quality of being secure; secureness. Specifically: (a) Freedom from apprehension, anxiety, or care; confidence of power of safety; hence, assurance; certainty. His trembling hand had lost the ease, Which marks security to please. Sir W. Scott. (b) Hence, carelessness; negligence; heedlessness.
secede: To withdraw from fellowship, communion, or association; to separate one's self by a solemn act; to draw off; to retire; especially, to withdraw from a political or religious body.
sentiently: In a sentient or perceptive way.
seriesturns: The turns in a series circuit.
senility: The quality or state of being senile; old age.
selfconsistent: Consistent with one's self or with itself; not deviation from the ordinary standard by which the conduct is guided; logically consistent throughout; having each part consistent with the rest.
separatory: 1. (Chem.) An apparatus used in separating, as a separating funnel. 2. (Surg.) A surgical instrument for separating the pericranium from the cranium. (old)
semilunar: Shaped like a half moon. Semilunar bone (Anat.), a bone of the carpus; the lunar. See Lunar, n. -- Semilunar, or Sigmoid, valves (Anat.), the valves at the beginning of the aorta and of the pulmonary artery which prevent the blood from flowing back into the ventricle.
semiflosculous: Having all the florets ligulate, as in the dandelion.
semi: A prefix signifying half, and sometimes partly or imperfectly; as, semiannual, half yearly; semitransparent, imperfectly transparent. Note: The prefix semi is joined to another word either with the hyphen or without it. In this book the hyphen is omitted except before a capital letter; as, semiacid, semiaquatic, semi-Arian, semiaxis, semicalcareous.
semite: One belonging to the Semitic race. Also used adjectively. [Written also Shemite.]
semiofficial: Half official; having some official authority or importance; as, a semiofficial statement. -- Sem`i*of*fi"cial*ly, adv.
seagait: A long, rolling swell of the sea. Ham. Nav. Encyc.
serratirostral: Having a toothed bill, like that of a toucan.
selfconsistency: The quality or state of being self-consistent.
seta: 1. (Biol.) Any slender, more or less rigid, bristlelike organ or part; as the hairs of a caterpillar, the slender spines of a crustacean, the hairlike processes of a protozoan, the bristles or stiff hairs on the leaves of some plants, or the pedicel of the capsule of a moss. 2. (Zoöl.) (a) One of the movable chitinous spines or hooks of an annelid.
securiform: Having the form of an ax hatchet.
seagoing: Going upon the sea; especially, sailing upon the deep sea; -- used in distinction from coasting or river, as applied to vessels.
semipupa: The young of an insect in a stage between the larva and pupa.
sextuple: 1. Six times as much; sixfold. 2. (Mus.) Divisible by six; having six beats; as, sixtuple measure.
seamy: Having a seam; containing seams, or showing them. "Many a seamy scar." Burns. Everything has its fair, as well as its seamy, side. Sir W. Scott.
semiformed: Half formed; imperfectly formed; as, semiformed crystals.
servile: 1. Of or pertaining to a servant or slave; befitting a servant or a slave; proceeding from dependence; hence, meanly submissive; slavish; mean; cringing; fawning; as, servile flattery; servile fear; | An element which forms no part of the original root; -- opposed to radical.
servitude: 1. The state of voluntary or compulsory subjection to a master; the condition of being bound to service; the condition of a slave; slavery; bondage; hence, a state of slavish dependence. You would have sold your king to slaughter, His princes and his peers to servitude. Shak. A splendid servitude; . . . for he that rises up early, and goeSouth. 2. Servants, collectively.
selfdiscipline: Correction or government of one's self for the sake of improvement.
selfindulgent: Indulging one's appetites, desires, etc., freely.
sexlocular: Having six cells for seeds; six-celled; as, a sexlocular pericarp.
selfmade: Made by one's self. Self-made man, a man who has risen from poverty or obscurity by means of his own talentss or energies.
septuagenarian: A person who is seventy years of age; a septuagenary.
sense: 1. (Physiol.) A faculty, possessed by animals, of perceiving external objects by means of impressions made upon certain organs (sensory or sense organs) of the body, or of perceiving changes in the… | To perceive by the senses; to recognize. [Obs. or Colloq.] Is he sure that objects are not otherwise sensed by others than they are by him Glanvill.
seamstress: A woman whose occupation is sewing; a needlewoman.
setfair: In plastering, a particularly good troweled surface. Knight.
seemer: One who seems; one who carries or assumes an appearance or semblance. Hence shall we see, If power change purpose, what our seemers be. Shak.
sedge: 1. (Bot.) Any plant of the genus Carex, perennial, endogenous herbs, often growing in dense tufts in marshy places. They have triangular jointless stems, a spiked inflorescence, and long grasslike leaves which are usually rough on the margins and midrib. There are several hundred species.
sentimentalize: To regard in a sentimental manner; as, to sentimentalize a subject. | To think or act in a sentimental manner, or like a sentimentalist; to affect exquisite sensibility. C. Kingsley.
selfasserting: asserting one's self, or one's own rights or claims; hence, putting one's self forward in a confident or assuming manner.
setchisel: A kind of chisel or punch, variously shaped, with a broad flat end, used for stripping off rivet heads, etc.
sesquialtera: A stop on the organ, containing several ranks of pipes which reënforce some of the high harmonics of the ground tone, and make the sound more brilliant.
serolin: (a) A peculiar fatty substance found in the blood, probably a mixture of fats, cholesterin, etc. (b) A body found in fecal matter and thought to be formed in the intestines from the cholesterin of the bile; -- called also stercorin, and stercolin.
seismograph: An apparatus for registering the shocks and undulatory motions of earthquakes.
selfmotion: Motion given by inherent power, without external impulse; spontaneus or voluntary motion. Matter is not induced with self-motion. Cheyne.
seaturtle: (a) Any one of several very large species of chelonians having the feet converted into paddles, as the green turtle, hawkbill, loggerhead, and leatherback. They inhabit all warm seas. (b) The sea pigeon, or guillemot.
secretary: 1. One who keeps, or is intrusted with, secrets. 2. A person employed to write orders, letters, dispatches, public or private papers, records, and the like; an official scribe, amanuensis, or writer; one who attends to correspondence, and transacts other business, for an association, a public body, or an individual.
selective: Selecting; tending to select. This selective providence of the Almighty. Bp. Hall.
